narrative:
The model estimates a 53% chance that you will leave your current role, which is just over the threshold for predicting departure. As a result, the organization has decided not to offer you the promotion at this time.

Three factors stood out most strongly in the model’s reasoning. First, having received other job opportunities while working here pushed the prediction noticeably toward leaving. Employees who stay rarely report outside offers, so this signal carried significant weight. Second, your overall career experience of more than 11 years also increased the likelihood of departure. While most employees predicted to stay have between one and five years of total experience, your longer track record makes the model see you as someone who is more mobile in the job market. Third, the six to ten years you have already spent in this specific organization worked in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction back toward staying. This length of service is longer than what most stayers have, and the model interprets it as a sign of loyalty that slightly offsets the other two factors.

Taken together, the combination of external opportunities and your broad experience outweighed the stabilizing effect of your tenure here, tipping the balance just enough to forecast that you are likely to leave.

The organization should discuss retention measures with you, such as clearer advancement paths or adjusted compensation. You may also want to reflect on whether your current role still aligns with your long-term goals. Addressing these points openly could change the outlook for both sides. (248 words)
